title: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond
description: Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?So-called "job ghosting" has become a
body: Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training -  those dubbed as Neets - this week. Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."I've spent all that time and energy submitting my application but got nothing in return."Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.The 24-year-old says her biggest challenge throughout the job-hunting process has been not getting feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.She says she has also been ghosted after interviews several times."With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.The Milburn report, external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications."It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, a 21-year-old, from Swindon.Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances. But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this. Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says."It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting. But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.

schema.headline: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond

title: David Raya injury: Goalkeeper taken off during Newcastle 2-2 Arsenal
description: Injuries are never good news, but Arsenal's latest one to first-choice goalkeeper David Raya has come in the worst possible position.The 31-year-old w
body: Injuries are never good news, but Arsenal's latest one to first-choice goalkeeper David Raya has come in the worst possible position.The 31-year-old was forced to leave the pitch 70 minutes into Saturday's 2-2 draw with Newcastle, appearing to hurt his shoulder in an innocuous challenge with Magpies forward William Osula.The Gunners arguably have the best depth in the league with at least two quality options in all outfield positions after a period of squad strengthening.In goal, however, cover appears much thinner.Raya was a key component in Arsenal's Premier League title-winning campaign last season, was named in the Fifpro Men's World 11 and was unlucky to not win the Yashin Trophy, awarded to the world's best goalkeeper, which went to Spain team-mate Unai Simon.Behind him, Kepa Arrizabalaga still holds the record as the most expensive goalkeeper in football history following his £72m move from Athletic Bilbao to Chelsea in August 2018, but is far behind Raya in terms of quality.Raya's passing range and ability on the ball are key to how Arsenal build their attacks, and his presence is a big reason why they have the best defence in the league.They have conceded just seven Premier League goals this season, with only Brighton able to match that tally - having played a game fewer.Arsenal also brought in former Leeds goalkeeper Illan Meslier on a free transfer in the summer but his only appearance this season came in the embarrassing Carabao Cup defeat by League Two Fleetwood.When asked about Raya's injury, Arteta said he did not know how severe the issue is. "Well, unfortunately, he had to come off, which is never good news," said Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta. "He will get assessed now, and probably he will have an MRI [scan] tomorrow to see what it is exactly he has done."I don't know how it happened, and what the injury is at the moment, so we'll have to wait and see tomorrow." Arsenal are about to enter a gruelling period of games - with or without Raya.In the next four weeks, they face Borussia Dortmund, Manchester City, Brentford, Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid."The one player that Arsenal cannot afford to lose is David Raya," said former England forward Alan Shearer, who is a pundit on Saturday's BBC Match of the Day. "He has made such a difference since joining from Brentford in 2023."They have top-class cover in just about every other position but he is the one individual that Mikel Arteta will be thinking 'we don't want to play without him for an extended period'. They could, of course go into the transfer market if they need to in January, but Arteta will be desperately hoping Raya is not out for long."Raya is reportedly close to agreeing a new deal at the club, which shows his importance to the Gunners with two years remaining on his contract.Ex-England midfielder Jamie Redknapp said on Sky Sports that Raya is "irreplaceable"."Kepa is not up to the level of him - I actually think he struggles in the Premier League," added Redknapp. "Obviously we've seen in the Carabao Cup last year in the final."He is now going to have to play some games and that's going to be difficult for him."It will change everything for Arsenal for a while so that's a massive blow depending on how long David Raya is out because he is irreplaceable - probably the best goalkeeper in the Premier League, if not one of the best in the world."

schema.headline: David Raya injury: Goalkeeper taken off during Newcastle 2-2 Arsenal

title: Nations Championship: Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable with 20-17 win over South Africa
description: After six deflating losses in a row to South Africa, New Zealand and France, Andy Farrell was asked this week what made him think Ireland could get ba
body: After six deflating losses in a row to South Africa, New Zealand and France, Andy Farrell was asked this week what made him think Ireland could get back to the levels they had reached when considered squarely among that group.Because they had got there before came the typically uncomplicated response from the side's head coach.The longer the 2023 World Cup receded into memory, however, fewer and fewer believed that his side still had within them the type of performance they produced to beat the Springboks 20-17 on Saturday. Undoubtedly Ireland's biggest win of recent years, having not beaten one of the three sides who started this weekend above them in the rankings since the summer of 2024, this was one of their most needed too.This Test had long been viewed as one of the crucial measuring sticks for Farrell's side building towards next autumn's World Cup - the last time they will face the back-to-back champions before boarding the plane to Australia. Having settled into a pattern where they could not beat the best, but almost always found a way past the rest, Ireland could not have headed down under with genuine belief of making history without first showing they were still capable of this level. "It's something that we've been looking forward to, to challenge ourselves and delivering when it matters against top-line sides," said Farrell."We knew that this fixture was coming, playing against the world's best by a stretch at this moment in time"It was a game that we we wanted to challenge ourselves and see how we went and, obviously fronting up and showing the character that we did, and coming out on the right side of the win is a big night for everyone who is Irish."For all that had gone on in the build-up, from explosive news conferences to coaching suspensions, from dismissed citing complaints to eye-catching positional switches, by the time of kick-off, it almost felt as if a reminder was needed that there was still a game to be played.Some two hours later, with the banned Rassie Erasmsus having watched on from a nearby hotel with only a host of virtual followers on a near-silent YouTube stream for company, his Springboks side had lost consecutive games for the first time in four years.If his comments this week were designed to illicit a response from his side after last week's loss to France, he did not get the desired reaction. Instead, it was Ireland who it seemed had appropriately fuelled the fire.Virtually scrummaged off the park in this fixture last year, prop Andrew Porter was among those who said that day had stuck with them in the months since.While the tables were not turned at scrum-time, rather than allow the set-piece to again become the dominant thread of the game, this time around Ireland weathered the storm and came out the other side.Their aerial work in particular was key, with Farrell typically highlighting Robert Baloucoune's efforts to regather possession before mentioning the winger's second double in as many weeks."We were very good at just getting on with it," added the head coach."It's not always going to go your way against the world's best, certainly at scrum-time, they're world-leading in that regard. We took everything in isolation and just kept going on to the next moment."That was the story of the game, really."Even if South Africa had wrestled the game back in those frantic closing moments, this would not have been a loss to catalogue alongside the others against South Africa, France and New Zealand in recent years.Having started 2026 with their intent questioned after defeat in Paris, Ireland played their last home game of the year showing an appreciation that in these sorts of contests, it is the small moments that make for big results. A first-half scrum penalty of their own was greeted as raucously as a score while, whether it be a Joe McCarthy maul turnover, Mack Hansen's try-saving tackle on Canan Moodie or Hugo Keenan eating up the ground to thwart Kurt-Lee Arendse, Ireland continued to show that this time they were to stay in the fight. There will still be talk of whether this was truly Ireland absorbing South Africa's best punch - with both the Boks and All Blacks having lost twice in succession, questions will be asked of how much the four-Test Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series has taken out of both sides. "We're not playing to our best potential," said captain Siya Kolisi."We know as a group we have better. I don't question the effort or the mindset, but it's executing better."Still, Ireland must believe that this was a game that said more about themselves than their opponents.

schema.headline: Nations Championship: Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable with 20-17 win over South Africa

title: Wales 26-29 Australia: Wallabies hold on for Nations Championship win in Cardiff
description: Australia hold on for narrow win against WalesImage source, Huw Evans Picture AgencyImage caption, Australia secured a record win against Wales on the
body: Australia hold on for narrow win against WalesImage source, Huw Evans Picture AgencyImage caption, Australia secured a record win against Wales on their previous visit to Cardiff in 2024ByGareth GriffithsBBC Sport WalesNations ChampionshipWales (7) 26Tries: Lake 2, Murray, Elias Cons: Costelow 3Australia (12) 29Tries: Tupou, Paenga-Amosa, Jorgensen, Ikitau Cons: Lonergan 2, Gordon Pens: GordonWales could not emulate their famous victory against New Zealand as Australia claimed the Nations Championship spoils in Cardiff.The Wallabies ended a four-match losing run thanks to tries from hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa, prop Taniela Tupou, wing Max Jorgensen and centre Len Ikitau, while fly-half Carter Gordon kicked a late penalty.Wales captain Dewi Lake scored two tries, while full-back Blair Murray also crossed following a superb assist by wing Louis Rees-Zammit.Replacement hooker Ryan Elias grabbed a late try but Australia held on for victory as Wales paid the price for not capitalising on attacking chances.Wales finished fifth in the northern hemisphere section and will play Japan at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Saturday (13:10 GMT).Australia finished third in the southern hemisphere table and play Ireland on Friday (20:10 GMT).Fans flock back to the Principality StadiumFigure caption, Highlights: Wallabies edge Wales in CardiffAfter all the hysteria and celebrations to mark a first victory against the All Blacks in 73 years, the attention turned towards whether Wales could back it up against Australia.There was a vibrancy on the streets of Cardiff before the game not seen for a while, which reflected in the crowd.After crowds of 52,425 against Japan and 55,152 against New Zealand, the 66,307 attendance against Australia was the highest of the autumn.The All Blacks win proved instrumental in a surge of tickets sold for a 20:10 GMT kick-off, the latest for a Wales rugby home game at the Principality Stadium.Head coach Steve Tandy made four changes to revert to the side that beat Japan with flanker James Botham the most notable absentee following his player-of-the-match against New Zealand.Botham was expecting the birth of his first child this week but Tandy stated his omission was for rugby reasons with Cardiff colleague Alex Mann replacing him.Fit-again number eight Aaron Wainwright replaced Taine Basham, while lock Ben Carter and wing Josh Adams returned for Adam Beard and Gabriel Hamer-Webb.Australia had freshened things up with five forward changes as flanker Carlo Tizzano, lock Tom Hooper and the front-row trio of Isaac Kailea, Paenga-Amosa and Tupou came in.Australia open scoring after Llewellyn yellow cardWales lost centre Max Llewellyn inside two minutes to a yellow card for a high tackle on Wallabies full-back Tom Wright.Wallabies had plenty of early possession against 14 players but the home defence comfortably dealt with the attack.Mann was caught with some friendly fire by a finger in the eye from team-mate Carter but continued despite appearing to have vision issues.Rees-Zammit almost squeezed into the corner but just failed to ground the ball under pressure from Gordon, before Lake was held up over the Australia line.Mann, despite his eye seeming to be closing, was still able to force a turnover penalty but Wales were guilty of early handling errors.After Wales won a scrum penalty, the officials then either missed Tupou striking Mann with a body jab, or deemed it did not warrant further action. Tupou stayed on the field to open the scoring in the 21st minute as he evaded Llewellyn's tackle to cross for an unconverted try.Wales bounce back but Wallabies lead at half-time Image source, Huw Evans Picture AgencyImage caption, Wales captain Dewi Lake has now scored 12 tries in 37 internationalsWales retaliated quickly with Morgan breaking away and feeding scrum-half Tomos Williams, who was held up by superb visiting defence.There were important turnover penalties from Tizzano and Tupou who benefitted from a huge tackle from Australia captain Harry Wilson on opposite number Wainwright.The hosts held the upper hand in the first-half aerial battle but Wales were not as clinical as they were against New Zealand.Australia centre Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii gained an intercept before being hauled down by Rees-Zammit, who conceded a penalty.Wallabies demonstrated a more ruthless approach as Paenga-Amosa was driven over. Mann continued to wind up the Australia forwards, which helped gain 10 metres for dissent, but Wales continued to waste chances as an attacking line-out was stolen.Morgan was a Wales carrying colossus in the first half with a series of impressive bursts and the home side finally gained a reward in the 40th minute when Lake dived over with Costelow converting.Australia led 12-7 at half-time with Wales having an on-pitch huddle before heading to their changing room.Wallabies aerial dominance proves crucialSuaalii towered over Murray to take an early second-half attacking high ball but Wallabies were denied a try by a brilliant Morgan turnover.Australia scrum-half Lonergan missed a penalty before Wallabies' second-half aerial  dominance was rewarded when Jorgensen rose above Adams before finishing off the move to score.Wales brought on a raft of replacements, including an early introduction for scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams.The changes worked when Lake was driven over for his second score before Wales followed up with a magical try.Rees-Zammit was the architect with a stunning outside break before feeding Adams who provided the try-scoring pass to Murray. Costelow's conversion gave Wales the lead for the first time.Figure caption, Murray with try of the Nations Championship?Australia hold on for first win in five matchesAustralia brought on experienced forward replacements with Fraser McReight and Angus Bell making immediate impacts.Prop Allan Alaalatoa appeared to have scored on his 99th international, but it was ruled out following a knock-on by replacement scrum-half Kalani Thomas.The Wallabies wave continued with Wales duo Eddie James and Archie Griffin producing impressive tackles before Ikitau restored the visitors' lead.Morgan left the field for a head injury assessment (HIA) to be replaced by Kane James, who was in tears when the anthem was played as he marked his first Wales appearance in Cardiff.Fellow replacement Louie Hennessey knocked on to give Australia an attacking platform before Wainwright conceded a penalty which Carter kicked to take the Wallabies two scores clear.Morgan returned and Wales responded as they battered the Australia line with Wilson shown a yellow card.Elias was driven over to secure two losing bonus-points and set up a grandstand finale, but Wallabies held on for a vital victory for head coach Les Kiss.Line-upsWales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, E James, Llewellyn, Adams; Costelow, T Williams; Smith, Lake (capt), Griffin, Jenkins, Carter, Mann, Morgan, Wainwright.Replacements: Elias, G Thomas, Lewis, Plumtree, K James, Morgan-Williams, Hawkins, Hennessey.Yellow card: Llewellyn 2Australia: Wright; Jorgensen, Suaalii, Ikitau, Potter; Gorden, Lonergan; Kailea, Paenga-Amosa, Tupou, Canham, Hooper, Valetini, Tizzano, Wilson (capt).Yellow card: Wilson 79Replacements: Pollard, Bell, Alaalatoa, Williams, McReight, Thomas, Donaldson, Daugunu.Match officialsReferee: Luc Ramos (France).Assistant referees: Karl Dickson (England) & Jeremy Rozier (France).Television match official (TMO): Eric Gauzins (France).Foul play review officer (FPRO): Andrew Jackson (RFU).

schema.headline: Wales 26-29 Australia: Wallabies hold on for Nations Championship win in Cardiff

title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
description: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when
body: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight."She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue."He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen"."She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did."That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent."Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina."And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025. He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.But she kept any of those fears from Jenny."I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door."I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.He remains behind bars awaiting trial.A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her."Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away.""She's doing great for what she's gone through."They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen."I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

schema.headline: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl

title: COP31: New draft deal aims to avert collapse of talks at climate summit
description: Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggled to reach a new global climate deal.A new
body: Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggled to reach a new global climate deal.A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.And it includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.Countries were expected to reconvene at 09:00 local time (06:00GMT) to decide whether to approve a new deal.If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday. On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.

schema.headline: COP31: New draft deal aims to avert collapse of talks at climate summit

title: Freshers' flu left me deaf in both ears - I'm now helping people like me drive
description: Darcie, from Dronfield in Derbyshire, said she went to university a year early, at the age of 17, and became deaf in the first few weeks."I just had f
body: Darcie, from Dronfield in Derbyshire, said she went to university a year early, at the age of 17, and became deaf in the first few weeks."I just had freshers' flu, and it deteriorated my inner ear on both sides," she said.Darcie added: "I assumed that me not being able to hear was just part of the illness and I didn't know it was a medical emergency, so I didn't get it checked until a week later and I still couldn't hear."And that's when they told me, because it's been so long, we can't get it back."She said the condition was called sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSHL).Darcie said it was not easy doing a music degree but she had to "find ways around things". "So it didn't ruin in my life, it just changed how I had to do things," she added.However, Darcie said it was challenging finding someone who felt comfortable teaching her.She said: "I reached out to God knows how many driving instructors, and they all said the same thing of 'I'm not confident I can accommodate that'."So when I contacted Dave, I didn't say anything and he was like, 'yeah, no worries. I can fit you in this day'. "And then at the end I put, 'oh yeah, by the way, I'm deaf', and that was it - we had to work together because he'd never worked with a deaf person before."She said they soon found ways of working around her hearing loss.These included for the emergency stop when the instructor usually shouts "stop", he instead puts his hand out in front of him really quickly.Darcie said during the lessons, they realised they could help share this knowledge. She said: "If I'm having this problem, I know that there's gonna be other people that are gonna need instructors that are deaf aware, can maybe sign a little bit. "Me and Dave just looked at each other one day, and were like, 'we should make a course', and he goes, 'yeah, we should'."I created the course myself and I sent it to Dave, and he loved it."Dave Leverton, from Handley Driving School, said he made adaptations for Darcie's lessons, including adding an extra mirror in a position where she could see him."[This] meant that we could use some verbal communication," she said."Then Darcie taught me things... simple sign language that we could manage on the move so that she knew where she was going and what she was going to do. "It was a constant process of her teaching me so that I could teach her."Franki Oliver, audiology manager at the Royal National Institute for Deaf People, said: "If you suddenly lose your hearing - either in one or both of your ears - getting treatment quickly is key. A sudden change in hearing is not always serious, but it could be a medical emergency."Sudden hearing loss can affect one or both ears, can happen instantly or over the course of a few weeks, and you might also have tinnitus or balance problems."Causes vary, and can include ear wax build-up, infection or physical injury. Recovery depends on the cause and how badly you're affected."Getting urgent treatment for sudden hearing loss increases your chance of recovering your hearing."Additional reporting by Ian Skye

schema.headline: Freshers' flu left me deaf in both ears - I'm now helping people like me drive

title: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85
description: Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85. His family said he died in the early hours of Saturda
body: Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85. His family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness. Spitting Image was immensely popular and sometimes controversial, running from 1984-1996 across 18 seasons, and featured puppet caricatures of celebrities, politicians and royals, including former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother. "The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining," a family statement said."With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image," it added."Peter's creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention."The show won several awards, including one Bafta TV award and two Emmys and at its peak drew an audience of 15 million. Fluck was born in Cambridge in 1941, and created the show alongside childhood friend Roger Law, who he met while studying at Cambridge School of Art. Following school, both Fluck and Law moved to London and set up as freelance illustrators, and in 1976 set up their partnership 'Luck and Flaw' back in Cambridge."You could say we took the traditional newspaper editorial cartoon and put it on the screen," Fluck told ArtCornwall in an interview, external in 2006.He described the show as being shown "at the difficult time of 10 o'clock on a Sunday night when all politicians should have been in bed". Many of the characters included parodies of Thatcher's cabinet, with Douglas Hurd depicted with "Mr Whippy ice cream" hair, and her successor John Major caricatured as a dull, grey puppet with a penchant for peas."We did get quite a lot of approaches from politicians for their puppet to be made, because if you didn't appear as a puppet on Spitting Image you hadn't made it as a politician," Fluck said in an interview in 2011. , externalIt was eventually axed by ITV because of declining audience numbers. In a statement, the broadcaster said Fluck's "creative contribution to TV satire is simply unrivalled... his cutting edge puppetry and caricature skills, alongside the show's sharp and always shrewdly observed humour, became a defining part of the cultural zeitgeist. "Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with his family and friends at this very sad time."When he stepped away from the show, Fluck moved to Cornwall and focused his art on ceramics, printmaking and mobiles. In 2018, Law donated his entire archive of Spitting Images to Cambridge University.The collection - including original scripts, puppet moulds, drawings and recordings - was conserved and held in the library.

schema.headline: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85

title: Princess of Wales: Catherine talks about her cancer journey in new documentary Heal
description: Catherine talks openly about how cancer changed her in documentary on BBCFigure caption, Watch: Trailer for new programme detailing Princess Catherine
body: Catherine talks openly about how cancer changed her in documentary on BBCFigure caption, Watch: Trailer for new programme detailing Princess Catherine's cancer journeyByRoyal correspondentThe Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC."It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day."It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William."It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.Image source, Matt Porteous/Kensington PalaceImage caption, Kensington Palace shared a photo of Catherine doing the Three Peaks Challenge, ahead of the documentaryCatherine has never disclosed what type of cancer she faced, but in March 2024 she revealed that she had a diagnosis of cancer and was receiving chemotherapy.In January 2025 she announced that she was in remission and in the following months began a gradual return to royal duties.She has often spoken about her different understanding of life after her illness, and the need to take a more holistic approach to well-being beyond physical recovery.The princess has talked about the good days and bad days that followed her treatment - and wanted to dispel the idea that patients could immediately return to how they felt before their illness.This documentary, which will be introduced by Kirsty Young, promises to be the fullest and most personal account of that journey, with her own insights into the impact such illness can have and how she found her own healing process.She has since returned to working for her charities and earlier this week was in India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony with Prince William, the first time they had travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Catherine visited India for William's Earthshot Prize which was hosted in Mumbai - the first time she'd been at the Earthshot awards since 2022Among the film crew for the documentary, as director of photography, was Will Warr, who has worked with Catherine and her family before.His pictures have been used in a video birthday message by Catherine and a Christmas card which showed a relaxed image of the princess and Prince William and their children.The filmmaker also made the personal video statement that marked the end of her chemotherapy in September 2024, with her message: "Out of darkness, can come light."Kate Phillips, the BBC's chief content officer, said it was hoped the 30-minute documentary "will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges".Catherine was treated at The Royal Marsden Hospital and funds from the distribution of this documentary, which is to be broadcast in other countries, will be paid to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.When cancer patients finish treatment at the London hospital they can symbolically ring a bell."I didn't ring the bell," says Catherine, speaking to her brother James Middleton."Maybe this is your ringing the bell," he says, about carrying out the Three Peaks Challenge and this documentary about her healing.Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November. It will also air internationally, including on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November, Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December

schema.headline: Princess of Wales: Catherine talks about her cancer journey in new documentary Heal

title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
description: A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and F
body: A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment."War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

schema.headline: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland

title: France 45-17 Argentina - Les Bleus secure final spot
description: Nations ChampionshipFrance (14) 45Tries: Guillard, Mauvaka, Gourgues 2, Gailleton, Duguid, Bielle-Biarrey Cons: Gourgues 5Argentina (10) 17Tries: Picc
body: Nations ChampionshipFrance (14) 45Tries: Guillard, Mauvaka, Gourgues 2, Gailleton, Duguid, Bielle-Biarrey Cons: Gourgues 5Argentina (10) 17Tries: Piccardo, Matera Cons: Albornoz 2 Pen: AlbornozFrance dispatched Argentina in Paris to book their spot against South Africa in the Nations Championship final at Allianz Stadium next Sunday.Knowing pre-game a bonus-point victory at Stade de France would be enough to edge England out of the top spot in the northern hemisphere standings, Les Bleus had to work hard to secure the points required.Lock Mickael Guillard powered over for the opening score, but Justo Piccardo responded for the visitors before Tomas Albornoz nudged them ahead with a penalty.Argentina have not been at their best this November, suffering a heavy defeat by Ireland before narrowly beating Italy.However, as is often the case with the Pumas, the longer they spend together, the more they tend to improve as a campaign progresses.Felipe Contepomi's side brought the first-half physicality needed to trouble France, who turned to their maul late in the first half to score through Peato Mauvaka and reclaim the lead.Fly-half Matthieu Jalibert, who missed the win over the world champions through injury, then expertly sent Kalvin Gourgues through a gap to score.The pivotal moment came when Argentina prop Mayco Vivas was shown a 20-minute red card for making direct head contact at a ruck, with France capitalising on the extra man to score their bonus-point try through Emilien Gailleton.Hooker Julian Montoya then joined Vivas in the sin-bin after receiving a yellow card and France made their numerical advantage count once again as Tyler Duguid and Gourgues crossed.Pablo Matera intercepted Louis Bielle-Biarrey's pass to improve the scoreline but Bielle-Biarrey made amends to dot down a brilliant kick into space by Antoine Dupont.It will now be rematch of last Friday's epic game in Paris, which France narrowly won 21-19 against the world champions.South Africa booked their spot in the final by picking up a losing bonus point against Ireland.Scotland will play Argentina on Sunday at Allianz Stadium in the seventh/eighth-place play-off.France: Attissogbe; Grandidier-Nkanang, Gourgues, Moefana, Bielle-Biarrey; Jalibert, Dupont (capt); Jelonch, Ollivon, Capilla; Guillard, Verhaeghe; Falatea, Mauvaka, GrosReplacements: Lamothe, Poirot, Montagne, Duguid, Woki, Alldritt, Lucu, GailletonArgentina: Prisciantelli; Delguy, Cinti, Chocobares, Mendy; Albornoz, Benitez Cruz; Isa, Scelzo, Gonzalez; Lavanini, Petti; Moreno, Montoya (capt), WengerReplacements: Bosch, Vivas, Sclavi, Elias, Rubiolo, Matera, Moyano, IsgroSin bin: Vivas (61 mins), Montoya (67 mins)

title: Newspaper headlines: Kate's 'road to recovery' and 'Brave princess'
description: The Mail on Sunday reports, external the Prince of Wales may strip his brother the Duke of Sussex of his titles when he becomes king, according to an
body: The Mail on Sunday reports, external the Prince of Wales may strip his brother the Duke of Sussex of his titles when he becomes king, according to an upcoming book. Citing the royal author Tom Sykes, the paper says Prince William is planning a "radical shake-up of the monarchy", which would include HRH titles only being granted to working royals. A spokesperson for the Prince and Catherine, Princess of Wales said they do not comment on claims made in books.Several front pages feature photos of Kate ahead of next weekend's BBC documentary in which she discusses her cancer recovery. The Daily Star Sunday, external describes her as "our queen of hearts", saying she has used her public profile "to raise money and awareness" for others. The Sunday Telegraph, external describes her as "grinning and winning" - a reference to her Three Peaks hiking challenge for charity.Lord Blunkett has a warning for Andy Burnham in the Sun on Sunday, external - after the prime minister moved to forge closer ties with the European Union on Friday. The former Labour minister describes himself as "sceptical", arguing that "the electorate are not yet ready for even bolder moves to integration". Alan Johnson, who launched Labour's 2016 campaign to remain in the EU, has a similar warning for the prime minister in the Sunday Mirror, external. He tells the paper another referendum "would be very damaging".The Sunday Times leads, external on its joint investigation with the BBC into the case of a man who killed three people in Exeter while suffering from a psychotic episode in 2019. The paper says the victims were "killed after police incompetence" - as warnings about the man's behaviour were ignored. Devon and Cornwall police says it is addressing "areas of learning".The late author, Dame Jilly Cooper, is accused of plagiarism in claims carried by the Observer, external. The paper says a "detailed analysis" of her fifth book "Prudence" shows that she copiously plundered two other novels - The Serial by Cyra McFadden and Josephine Tey's The Franchise Affair. Her agent and publisher did not respond to the paper's request for comment.And finally, a "Twickenham trouncing" is how the Sunday Express, external describes England's record win against New Zealand in rugby union's Nations Championship. The Sun on Sunday calls the 37-12 triumph Steve Borthwick's "finest moment" as head coach. For the Mail on Sunday, it was a performance of "total domination".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: Kate's 'road to recovery' and 'Brave princess'

title: The Witch Farm: Danny Robins drama inspired by 'real-life ghost story'
description: Robins, best-known for his podcast Uncanny, said the idea for the new drama came after he made The Battersea Poltergeist podcast for the BBC, which he
body: Robins, best-known for his podcast Uncanny, said the idea for the new drama came after he made The Battersea Poltergeist podcast for the BBC, which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story"."It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel," he said, which led him to discover the story of Liz and Bill Rich.In 1989, the young couple moved their family into a remote farmhouse at the foot of a mountain. They claimed to have experienced poltergeist activity, apparitions, alleged possessions and even physical injury.They say this lasted for seven years and changed them forever, as well as affecting the community around them.Robins said: "The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm. "Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary.After finishing the podcast, Robins asked himself "what's next?", admitting that telling the story as a TV documentary "didn't feel right", leading to the decision to dramatise it instead.Asked what he hopes viewers will feel when they watch the series, Robins said: "I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it."It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast."He also hopes that viewers will "laugh a little", adding that "humour has always been important" to his work.Robins also hopes to raise the question - "do ghosts exist?", sparking the debate between belief and scepticism."What's crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions," he said.The upcoming drama, which was filmed in Wales, stars Port Talbot-born actress Gabrielle Creevy, who recently starred in the new season of spy thriller Black Doves where she also uses her Welsh accent.She said: "I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same."Robins said she brought "absolute authenticity to the role" through her Welsh accent."Robins said The Witch Farm was "such a Welsh story", which was considered throughout making the production.He said an "almost entirely Welsh" crew was used in its creation, adding: "It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales."The Witch Farm will be available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from 22 November

schema.headline: The Witch Farm: Danny Robins drama inspired by 'real-life ghost story'

title: I Am Helen: Nicola Coughlan on her uncomfortable new TV drama
description: I Am Helen is the latest project in director Dominic Savage's I Am... series, female-led stories focusing on themes like mental health and relationshi
body: I Am Helen is the latest project in director Dominic Savage's I Am... series, female-led stories focusing on themes like mental health and relationships.The two fully-improvised episodes, devised in collaboration with Coughlan, follow a relationship spiralling after Steve tries to choke Helen during sex without consent."We never realised how incredibly timely it would be," Coughlan tells BBC Newsbeat. "We filmed this over a year ago."It feels incredibly relevant right now, and specifically right now, because pornography that includes strangulation has just been outlawed in the UK."Earlier this month, the government made it illegal for anyone to possess or publish porn that shows strangulation or suffocation.That decision followed a review last year that found choking was "rife" on porn sites and had become normalised, particularly among younger people.Coughlan and Cole say they were keen to make everything about their characters and the setting as relatable as possible to emphasise the shocking fallout."We needed one inciting incident that felt like something that could really plausibly happen between a couple, that it just goes slightly too far without consent, and it just blows everything up," Coughlan says."It's really important we see Steve's perspective in it because it makes him a normal guy."He's not this evil guy who's attacking Helen. He does bad things, but he's complicated. And hopefully you see them both as real people."Filming the series without a script meant the actors were fully immersed in their characters, making them real not just for viewers but for themselves too."I'm not playing myself, but there's far less, let's say 'character' here than anything else I've ever done because a lot of this is about just reacting," Coughlan says.She and Cole would film long takes, some lasting about an hour and often with heated exchanges, which might need to be shot multiple times.Coughlan describes I Am Helen as "the most challenging thing in terms of material that I've ever worked on", adding for the first time in a role she needed counselling."You literally would be physically and mentally quite exhausted," she says."There were times that I said to Dominic [Savage] if he wanted to do a third take for example - and I've never said this before on set - but I actually don't think I have that in me because you hit a wall."It's a lot to keep going."Cole agrees that "it was tough"."When you're given that freedom, things happen and I think you can get some really interesting and also quite shocking stuff," he says.For him, that came when he damaged a fridge on set with a punch.But it's that authenticity of emotion which, while difficult for the actors, is what Coughlan thinks makes the series so engaging."When people watch the 'I Ams', they feel quite truthful," she says."I think that's a big reason as to why, to be honest."Cole researched the manosphere online while developing his role and says he could see how people like Steve "quickly become lost in this quite simple ideology"."The more interesting thing was the lower level, the kind of 'bro influencer' type people, who a lot of what they say is actually quite good," he says. "You know, 'go to the gym, be healthy, look your best'."But occasionally they veer into comments on male and female societal roles and how a woman should stay at home."For someone like Steve, who Cole says wants a traditional relationship and a family, those ideas left him "completely lost".The characters quickly "get caught in a cycle", he says, as they find it harder and harder to understand each other."It starts off as a question, which becomes a debate, which becomes an argument, which becomes a huge bust-up, which becomes forgiveness, an apology, tears."Coughlan says viewers have told her they expected the series to end with serious violence, perhaps even with Steve killing Helen.But she was determined to avoid a shock factor so the characters didn't tip into being unrelatable."There's some very extreme moments in this, but some of them are not extreme," she says."It's better that he didn't [kill Helen] because as a viewer, you don't want people to go, 'well, if he does X, then that's the moment to leave'."From my perspective, you watch it and you go, 'you don't need to hit a threshold'."If you feel scared and uncomfortable, that's enough reason to get out of a situation."If you have been affected by the issues raised in this article, help and support is available via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: I Am Helen: Nicola Coughlan on her uncomfortable new TV drama
